hello.title: Hello, Dart
hello.summary: Write your first Dart program with void main and print, and work with strings and numbers.
hello.lesson.0: Every Dart program starts in a function called `main`. You write it as `void main()`, followed by curly braces `{ }`. The word `void` means that `main` gives back no value. The code between the braces runs from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.2: `print` shows a value and then starts a new line. Text in quotes, like `'Hello'`, is called a **string**. Dart accepts single quotes `'...'` and double quotes `"..."`; this course uses single quotes. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
hello.lesson.4: If you forget a semicolon, Dart reports an error and the program does not run at all. Dart is also case-sensitive: `Print` is not the same as `print`.
hello.lesson.6: Numbers do not need quotes. Dart calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses come first.
hello.lesson.8: The operator `/` always gives a decimal number: `7 / 2` is `3.5`, and `6 / 2` is `3.0`. The operator `~/` divides and drops the rest, so `7 ~/ 2` is `3`. The operator `%` gives the rest of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.
hello.lesson.11: For strings, `+` joins the text: `'2' + '3'` is `23`, not `5`. Inside a string, `\n` starts a new line.
hello.lesson.13: You cannot join a string and a number with `+`: `'Age: ' + 5` is an error. Unit 3 shows how to put numbers into strings.
hello.card.0: `void main() { }` is where the program starts
hello.card.1: `print(x);` shows `x` and starts a new line
hello-1.explain: `print` with a small `p` shows the value, and the statement ends with a semicolon. Without `;`, or with `Print` or `echo`, the program does not compile.
hello-3.explain: `17` divided by `5` is `3` with a rest of `2`. The operator `%` gives the rest.
hello-4.explain: The operator `/` always gives a decimal number. `10 / 4` is `2.5`.
hello-5.explain: `'4'` and `'5'` are strings because of the quotes. `+` joins strings, so the result is `45`.
hello-6.explain: `/` always gives a decimal number, so the program prints `4.0`. Use `8 ~/ 2` to get `4`.
hello-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3.
hello-7.explain: `~/` divides and drops the rest: `7 ~/ 2` is `3`. `/` gives `3.5`, `%` gives `1` and `*` gives `14`.
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that prints Hi, Dart!
hello-8.explain: `print('Hi, Dart!');` passes the string to `print` and ends the statement with `;`.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Ready, Set and Go on three lines.
hello-9.explain: The program starts with `void main() {` and ends with `}`. The statements in between run from top to bottom.

hello-12.explain: The string is not closed. Write `print('Done');` with a closing quote.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables with var, final and const, meet int, double, String and bool, and handle null.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. `var count = 3;` creates the variable `count` and stores `3` in it. The `=` stores a value; this is called **assignment**. Later you can store a new value without `var`. `count += 2` adds `2` to the variable, and `count++` adds `1`.
variables.lesson.2: Every value has a **type**. `int` is a whole number, `double` is a number with a decimal part, `String` is text and `bool` is `true` or `false`. With `var`, Dart works out the type from the value. You can also write the type instead of `var`.
variables.lesson.4: A variable keeps its type. After `var count = 3;`, the line `count = 'three';` is an error, because `count` is an `int`.
variables.lesson.6: A `final` variable gets its value only once. A `const` variable also never changes, and its value must be known before the program runs, for example a number written in the code. Use `final` or `const` for every value that does not change.
variables.lesson.9: The value `null` means "no value". Normal types like `int` and `String` can never hold `null`. Add a `?` to the type to allow it: a `String?` holds a string or `null`. A `String?` variable without a value starts as `null`.
variables.lesson.11: `int.tryParse('42')` turns a string into an `int`. If the string is not a number, it gives `null`, so its type is `int?`. Where Dart needs an `int`, you can write `!` after the value: it says "this is not `null`". If the value is `null` after all, the program stops with an error.
variables.card.0: `var x = 5;` creates a variable, Dart works out the type
variables.card.2: `final` is set once, `const` is fixed before the program runs
variables-1.explain: `x` starts as `4`, becomes `8` after `x * 2`, and `x += 1` adds `1`: `9`.
variables-2.explain: `4.5` has a decimal part, so it is a `double`. An `int` holds only whole numbers.
variables-3.explain: A `final` variable gets its value only once. The line `city = 'Oslo';` is an error, so the program does not run.
variables-4.explain: A `String?` variable without a value starts as `null`, and `print` shows `null`.
variables-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the variable can hold null.
variables-5.explain: Only a type with `?` can hold `null`. `String` cannot, and `String!` and `?String` are not valid types.
variables-6.explain: An `int` plus a `double` gives a `double`: `7 + 2.5` is `9.5`.
variables-7.explain: `count` is an `int` and cannot hold the string `'four'`. Write `count = 4;`.
variables-8.prompt: Build a line that creates a constant named limit with the value 10.
variables-8.explain: `const limit = 10;` creates a value that never changes. Dart has no `let`, and `==` compares instead of storing.
variables-9.prompt: Match the type or value with its meaning.
variables-9.pairs.1: a number with a decimal part
variables-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 15.
variables-10.explain: First create `total` with `10`, then add `5`, then print the result `15`.
variables-11.explain: `'7x'` is not a number, so `int.tryParse` gives `null`.
variables-12.statement: The value of a `const` variable must be known before the program runs.
variables-12.explain: `const` values are fixed in the code, like `const maxPlayers = 4;`. For a value that is calculated while the program runs, use `final`.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Put values into strings with $ and ${...}, and use length, toUpperCase, contains and substring.
strings.lesson.0: You can put a variable into a string with `$` and the name: `'Hello, $name!'`. Dart replaces `$name` with the value of `name`. This is called **string interpolation**, and it works with numbers too.
strings.lesson.2: For more than a name, use `${...}` with curly braces. Dart calculates what is inside the braces and puts the result into the string.
strings.lesson.5: A string knows things about itself. `.length` gives the number of characters. A **method** is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot and parentheses: `word.toUpperCase()` gives the string in capital letters, `word.toLowerCase()` in small letters.
strings.lesson.7: `contains` checks whether a string contains another string and gives `true` or `false`. `startsWith` checks the beginning. Capital and small letters count as different.
strings.lesson.10: Every character has a position, called its **index**. Counting starts at `0`, so `word[0]` is the first character. `substring(start, end)` gives the part from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Without `end`, it goes to the end of the string. `indexOf` gives the index where a part first appears.
strings.lesson.12: Strings never change. `word.toUpperCase()` gives a **new** string; `word` itself keeps its value. Store the result if you need it: `var big = word.toUpperCase();`.
strings.card.0: `'Hi, $name'` puts a variable into a string
strings.card.1: `'${a + b}'` puts a result into a string
strings.card.4: `s[0]` is the first character, `s.substring(1, 3)` a part
strings-1.explain: `$name` is replaced by the value of `name`, which is `Sam`.
strings-2.explain: Dart calculates `x * 2` inside `${...}`, which is `10`. The `x = ` outside the braces is normal text.
strings-4.explain: The index starts at `0`. `substring(1, 3)` takes the characters at index `1` and `2`: `a` and `r`.
strings-5.explain: Capital and small letters count as different. `'Paris'` does not contain `'paris'`, so it prints `false`.
strings-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints DART.
strings-6.explain: The method is called `toUpperCase`. The other names do not exist for strings in Dart.
strings-7.explain: `toUpperCase()` gives a new string, but the result is not stored. `s` still holds `'code'`.
strings-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the number of characters in name.
strings-8.explain: `print(name.length);` reads the `length` of the string and prints it.
strings-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Hello, Ada!
strings-9.explain: `first` must exist before it is used in `greeting`, and `greeting` must exist before it is printed.
strings-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
strings-10.pairs.4: the value of x inside a string
strings-11.prompt: The program should print Sum: 5. Which line has the bug?
strings-11.explain: `$a + b` puts only `a` into the string and keeps `+ b` as text. Write `print('Sum: ${a + b}');`.
strings-12.explain: The index starts at `0`: `b` is `0`, `a` is `1`, and the first `n` is at index `2`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program decide with if and else, comparisons, && and ||, switch, the ternary operator and ??.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses, the code in curly braces. The code after `else` runs when the condition is `false`.
conditions.lesson.2: Comparison operators give a `bool`: `==` means equal, `!=` not equal, `<` less than, `>` greater than, `<=` less than or equal, `>=` greater than or equal. Do not mix them up: `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values.
conditions.lesson.4: With `else if` you check another condition when the one before was `false`. Dart checks from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`.
conditions.lesson.6: Logical operators combine conditions: `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`, `||` (or) when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.9: `switch` compares one value with several `case` labels and runs the code of the matching one. Only that case runs; you do not need `break`. The `default` case runs when no case matches.
conditions.lesson.11: The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` gives `a` when the condition is `true`, and `b` otherwise. The operator `??` gives the value on the left, or the value on the right when the left one is `null`.
conditions.card.4: `c ? a : b` picks a value, `x ?? 'none'` replaces `null`
conditions-1.explain: `7 % 2` is `1`, so `x % 2 == 0` is `false` and the `else` block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `15 > 20` is `false`, `15 > 10` is `true`, so `mild` is printed. After that, Dart skips the rest.
conditions-3.statement: In Dart, `=` compares two values and `==` stores a value.
conditions-3.explain: It is the other way round: `=` stores a value in a variable, `==` compares two values.
conditions-4.explain: `5 > 3` is `true`, but `2 > 4` is `false`. `&&` needs both sides to be `true`.
conditions-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Welcome.
conditions-5.explain: `age >= 18` is `true` and `member` is `false`. Only `||` needs just one `true` side.
conditions-6.explain: `city` is `null`, so `??` gives the value on the right: `unknown`.
conditions-7.explain: `0 > 0` is `false`, so the ternary operator gives the value after `:`.
conditions-8.prompt: The program should print Equal. Which line has the bug?
conditions-8.explain: `=` stores a value; to compare, use `==`. Write `if (a == b) {`.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Big.
conditions-9.explain: Create `n` first. `50 > 10` is `true`, so `print('Big')` belongs in the `if` block and `print('Small')` in the `else` block.
conditions-10.prompt: Build a line that stores 'yes' in label when n is greater than 0, and 'no' otherwise.
conditions-10.explain: `condition ? a : b` gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` otherwise.

conditions-11.pairs.3: at least one side must be true

loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for, for-in, while and do-while, and control loops with break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop repeats code. `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)` has three parts, separated by semicolons: the start `var i = 0`, the condition `i < 3` that is checked before every round, and the step `i++` that runs after every round.
loops.lesson.2: The step can be anything that changes the variable. `i--` subtracts `1`, `i -= 3` subtracts `3`, and `i *= 2` multiplies by `2`.
loops.lesson.5: `for (var item in items)` runs once for every item of a list, from first to last. A list is written in square brackets, like `['apple', 'pear']`; you learn more about lists in unit 7.
loops.lesson.8: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. It checks the condition before every round, so it can also run zero times. Change a variable inside the loop, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.10: A `do` ... `while` loop runs its body first and checks the condition after it, so the body runs at least once. Note the semicolon after `while (...)`.
loops.lesson.12: `break` stops the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.
loops.card.1: `for (var x in items) { }` goes through every item
loops.card.2: `while (c) { }` checks first, `do { } while (c);` runs at least once
loops.card.3: `break` stops the loop, `continue` goes to the next round
loops-1.explain: The loop adds `1`, `2`, `3` and `4` to `total`: `1 + 2 + 3 + 4` is `10`.
loops-2.prompt: How many times does this program print Hi?
loops-2.explain: `i` takes the values `0`, `2` and `4`. At `6`, the condition `i < 5` is `false`, so the loop runs 3 times.
loops-3.explain: `n` goes from `1` to `3`, `9` and `27`. Then `27 < 20` is `false` and the loop stops.
loops-4.explain: `while` checks the condition first. `5 < 5` is `false`, so the body never runs and only `done` is printed.
loops-5.explain: A `do` ... `while` loop runs its body before it checks the condition, so `inside` is printed once.
loops-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints every fruit.
loops-6.explain: A for-in loop in Dart uses the keyword `in`: `for (var f in fruits)`.
loops-7.explain: `continue` skips `3`, so the sum is `1 + 2 + 4 + 5`, which is `12`.
loops-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 3, 2 and 1 on three lines.
loops-8.explain: Create `n` first. Inside the loop, print `n` before you make it smaller; otherwise it prints `2`, `1` and `0`.
loops-9.prompt: Build a loop header that makes i go from 0 to 4.
loops-9.explain: `for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {` starts at `0` and stops before `5`. With `i <= 5`, it would also run for `5`.
loops-10.prompt: The program should print 1, 2 and 3. Which line has the bug?
loops-10.explain: With `i < 3` the loop stops after `2`. Write `for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {`.
loops-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-11.pairs.1: goes on with the next round
loops-12.prompt: Which loop checks its condition only after the first round?
loops-12.explain: A `do` ... `while` loop runs the body first and checks the condition at the end. The other loops check before every round.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with return types, optional and named parameters, and the short arrow syntax =>.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run as often as you like. You already know `main`. You write your own functions outside of `main`: first the return type, then the name, then the **parameters** in parentheses. `void` means that the function gives back no value.
functions.lesson.2: `return` sends a value back to the code that called the function, and the function ends there. Write the type of that value before the name, for example `int add(int a, int b)`.
functions.lesson.5: When a function only returns one expression, you can use `=>`. `int square(int x) => x * x;` means the same as `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`.
functions.lesson.8: Parameters in square brackets `[ ]` are **optional**. You can leave them out when you call the function. Give them a default value with `=`, which is used when the value is missing.
functions.lesson.10: Parameters in curly braces `{ }` are **named**. When you call the function, you write the name and a colon, like `width: 3`, and the order does not matter. Named parameters are optional, unless you mark them with `required`.
functions.lesson.12: Dart checks the types of the parameters before the program runs. `add('2', 3)` is an error, because `add` needs two `int` values.
functions.card.0: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`
functions.card.1: `int square(int x) => x * x;` for one expression
functions.card.2: `void` means the function gives back no value
functions.card.4: `{required int x, int y = 0}` are named, call with `f(x: 1)`
functions-1.explain: The inner call `twice(3)` gives `6`, and `twice(6)` gives `12`.
functions-2.prompt: What does void before a function name mean?

functions-2.options.2: The function has no code inside
functions-2.options.3: The function can run only once
functions-2.explain: `void` is the return type for "no value". A `void` function can still have parameters and code, and you can call it as often as you like.
functions-3.explain: Positional parameters are filled in order: `a` is `3` and `b` is `10`, so `3 - 10` is `-7`.
functions-4.explain: The optional parameter `mark` is missing in the call, so its default value `'!'` is used.

functions-5.explain: `return` sends the value back to the caller. The other words do not return a value here.
functions-6.explain: `width` is missing, so it uses its default value `1`. `1 * 5` is `5`.

functions-7.explain: The function calculates `x * x` but never gives it back. Write `return x * x;`.
functions-8.prompt: Build an arrow function twice that gives back n times 2.
functions-8.explain: `int twice(int n) => n * 2;` is the short form of a function with one `return`.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so that total(1, 2) gives back 6.
functions-9.explain: First add the numbers (`3`), then double the sum (`6`), then return it. Code after `return` would never run.

collections.title: Collections
collections.summary: Keep many values in a List, a Map or a Set, change them, and transform lists with map and where.
collections.lesson.0: A **List** holds many values in a fixed order. You write it in square brackets `[ ]`, with commas between the values. `List<String>` means a list of strings. `names[0]` is the first item, because the index starts at `0`. `.length` gives the number of items, and `.last` the last item.
collections.lesson.2: `add` puts a value at the end of a list. `list[i] = value` replaces an item, and `remove` takes a value out. `contains` checks whether a value is in the list.
collections.lesson.4: You can go through a list with a for-in loop. `map` makes a new value from every item, and `where` keeps only the items for which a condition is `true`. Both take a short function, like `(n) => n * 2`. Add `.toList()` to get a list again.
collections.lesson.7: A **Map** stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**, in curly braces: `{'apple': 3}`. `stock['apple']` reads the value for a key; a missing key gives `null`. Assigning to a key adds or changes a pair. `<String, int>{}` is an empty map with `String` keys and `int` values.
collections.lesson.9: `.keys` gives all keys and `.values` all values; `print` shows them in round brackets. To go through the pairs, loop over `.entries`; every entry has a `key` and a `value`.
collections.lesson.12: A **Set** holds every value only once. You write it in curly braces with values only: `{'dart', 'code'}`. Adding a value that is already in the set changes nothing. An empty `{}` is a map, so write `<String>{}` for an empty set.
collections-1.explain: The index starts at `0`: `nums[0]` is `4`, `nums[1]` is `8`.
collections-2.explain: `add` puts `4` at the end, so the list has `4` items.
collections-3.explain: The key `'coffee'` is not in the map, so reading it gives `null`.
collections-4.explain: A set holds every value once. Adding `2` again changes nothing, so the set is `{1, 2, 3}` with `3` values.
collections-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints [2, 4].
collections-5.explain: `where` keeps the items for which the condition is `true`. `map` would give `[false, true, false, true]`, and `filter` does not exist in Dart.
collections-6.explain: `map` multiplies every item by `10`, and `toList()` makes a list of the results.
collections-7.prompt: Which code creates an empty Set of strings?
collections-7.explain: `{}` alone is an empty map, and square brackets make a list. `<String>{}` is an empty set of strings.
collections-8.prompt: The program should print blue. Which line has the bug?
collections-8.explain: The index starts at `0`, so the third item has index `2`. Write `print(colors[2]);`.
collections-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints {pen: 3, cup: 1}.
collections-9.explain: Create the empty map first. A map keeps the order in which you add the keys, so add `pen` before `cup`, then print.
collections-10.prompt: Build a line that adds 'kiwi' to the list fruits.
collections-10.explain: `fruits.add('kiwi');` puts `'kiwi'` at the end of the list. Dart lists have no `push` or `append`.

classes.title: Classes
classes.summary: Build your own types with classes: fields, constructors with this., methods, getters and toString.
classes.lesson.0: A **class** is a plan for your own type. It describes data, called **fields**, and actions, called **methods**. A value made from a class is an **object**. `Dog()` creates a new object of the class `Dog`. You reach its fields and methods with a dot.
classes.lesson.3: A **constructor** sets the fields when an object is created. It has the same name as the class. `Point(this.x, this.y);` takes two values and stores them in the fields `x` and `y`. The word `this` means the object itself. Fields that never change can be `final`.
classes.lesson.5: A constructor can also have named parameters, like a function: `Person({required this.name, this.age = 0});`. The caller writes the names, and missing values use their default.
classes.lesson.8: A **getter** looks like a field, but it calculates its value every time you read it. Write `get` before the name and no parentheses. You also read it without parentheses: `r.area`.
classes.lesson.10: When you print an object, Dart calls its method `toString`. Without your own version, it prints `Instance of 'Point'`. You write your own `toString` with `@override` in front; `@override` says that you replace a method that every class already has.
classes.card.1: `Point(this.x, this.y);` is a constructor that sets fields
classes.card.3: `int get sum => x + y;` is a getter, read as `p.sum`
classes-1.explain: `value` starts at `0`, and every call of `up()` adds `1`. After two calls it is `2`.
classes-2.explain: The constructor `Cat(this.name)` stores `'Tom'` in the field `name`, and `c.name` reads it.
classes-3.explain: `size` is `final`, so it cannot change after the constructor has set it. `b.size = 5;` is an error.
classes-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 5.
classes-4.explain: `this.x, this.y` stores the first value in `x` and the second in `y`. Without `this.`, the fields get no value, which is an error.
classes-5.explain: The getter `area` calculates `side * side`, which is `5 * 5 = 25`.
classes-6.explain: `Car` has no own `toString`, so Dart uses the default one, which prints `Instance of 'Car'`.
classes-7.prompt: The program should print 3.0. Which line has the bug?
classes-7.explain: The constructor must store the value in the field. Write `Circle(this.r);`.
classes-8.prompt: The class Counter has a field value that starts at 0 and a method up() that adds 1. Put the lines in order so the program prints 0 and then after: 1.
classes-8.explain: Create the object first. Print `value` while it is still `0`, then call `up()`, then print the new value.
classes-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a Point with x 3 and y 4 and stores it in p.
classes-9.explain: `var p = Point(3, 4);` calls the constructor with two values and stores the new object in `p`.
classes-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
classes-10.pairs.2: a value that is calculated when you read it
classes-10.pairs.3: the text shown when you print an object
classes-11.explain: `print` calls the own `toString` method, which puts `deg` into the string.
classes-12.explain: The named parameter `admin` is missing in the call, so it gets its default value `false`.
